decks.title: Electricity — Part 1: Current, potential difference and Ohm’s law
goals: Define electric current and potential difference and state their SI units
Calculate charge, number of electrons and work done using Q = It and V = W/Q
Draw circuit diagrams with standard symbols and connect an ammeter and a voltmeter correctly
State Ohm’s law and find resistance from a V–I graph

slides.heading: Electricity
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what flows in a wire, what pushes it, how we **draw and measure** circuits, and the simple rule that links them: **Ohm’s law**.
slides.narration: Namaste! Flick a switch and a fan starts, a phone charges, a room lights up. Behind all of it is a flow of tiny charged particles through wires, pushed by a battery or the mains supply. In this part we learn to describe that flow with numbers, draw circuits the way engineers do, and discover a rule that lets us predict the current in a circuit.

slides.heading: Electric current: the rate of flow of charge
slides.body_md: If a net charge $Q$ flows through any cross-section of a conductor in time $t$, the **electric current** is $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$. Its SI unit is the **ampere (A)**: **1 A = 1 C/s**.

visual.alt: Table: charge Q is measured in coulombs; current I in amperes, with milliampere equal to one thousandth and microampere one millionth of an ampere

slides.narration: Think of people walking through a gate at a cricket stadium. The current is not how many people there are, but how many pass the gate each second. In a wire, current is the amount of charge passing a point each second. One ampere means one coulomb of charge every second. Small currents, like those in a calculator, are measured in milliamperes.

slides.heading: Electrons move one way, current is shown the other
slides.body_md: In metal wires the moving charges are **electrons**. By convention, **electric current flows from + to −**, opposite to the flow of electrons.

slides.narration: When electricity was first studied, nobody knew about electrons, so scientists agreed to show current flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal. Later we learnt that in metals it is negative electrons that actually move, from the negative terminal towards the positive. We still use the old convention. The arrow on a circuit diagram always shows conventional current.

slides.heading: How much charge is a coulomb?
slides.body_md: The charge on one electron is $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C. A coulomb is the charge on about $6 \times 10^{18}$ electrons. If $n$ electrons pass, $Q = n e$.

visual.alt: Table: one electron carries 1.6 times ten to the minus nineteen coulomb; one coulomb is the charge of about 6.25 times ten to the eighteen electrons, the number passing a point each second in a current of one ampere

slides.narration: One electron carries an incredibly tiny charge. To make up just one coulomb you need about six million million million electrons. So even a small current of one ampere means billions upon billions of electrons drifting past every point of the wire each second. That is why we count charge in coulombs rather than in electrons.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: charge and electrons from a charger
slides.body_md: A phone charger supplies a steady current of **0.5 A** for **10 minutes**. Find the charge delivered and the number of electrons that flow.
bullets: Step 1 — convert time to seconds: $t = 10 \times 60 = 600$ s.
Check — about $2 \times 10^{21}$ electrons: a huge number, as expected for 300 C.

visual.alt: Table summarising the example: 0.5 ampere for 600 seconds gives 300 coulombs, which is about 1.9 times ten to the twenty-one electrons

slides.narration: Three habits will save you marks here. First, always convert minutes to seconds before using the formula. Second, write the formula before substituting. Third, give the unit with the answer. Notice how the number of electrons is enormous, while the charge in coulombs is a comfortable everyday number.

slides.heading: Quick check: charge in a minute
slides.body_md: A current of 2 A flows for 30 minutes. How much charge flows?
slides.narration: Quick check. Convert the time into seconds first, then multiply by the current.

slides.heading: Potential difference: the push
slides.body_md: Charges flow only if there is a **potential difference** across the conductor. The potential difference between two points is the **work done to move a unit charge** from one point to the other: $V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$. Its unit is the **volt**: **1 V = 1 J/C**.

visual.alt: Table of typical potential differences: a torch cell 1.5 volts, a phone battery about 3.7 volts, a car battery 12 volts and Indian household mains 220 volts

slides.narration: Water flows through a pipe only if there is a difference in pressure. In the same way, charges flow in a wire only if there is a difference of electric potential. A cell does chemical work to create this difference. A potential difference of one volt means one joule of work is done on every coulomb of charge moved between the two points.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: energy given to charge
slides.body_md: How much work is done in moving **20 C** of charge through a potential difference of **9 V**?
bullets: Check — each coulomb gains 9 J; 20 coulombs gain $20 \times 9$ J.

visual.alt: Table: potential difference 9 volts, charge 20 coulombs, work done 180 joules

slides.narration: Read the volt as joules per coulomb and the answer almost writes itself. A nine volt battery gives nine joules to every coulomb that passes through it. Twenty coulombs therefore receive one hundred and eighty joules. That energy then appears as light, heat or motion in whatever the battery is driving.

slides.narration: To measure the current through the bulb, the current must pass through the meter, so the ammeter goes in series. To measure the potential difference across the bulb, the voltmeter is connected across its two ends, in parallel. In both meters, the positive terminal should be joined to the side that leads back to the positive terminal of the cell.

So it draws almost no current

visual.alt: Comparison table: an ammeter measures current, is connected in series and has very low resistance; a voltmeter measures potential difference, is connected in parallel and has very high resistance

slides.narration: A good meter should not disturb what it measures. An ammeter sits in the path of the current, so it must have a very low resistance, or it would reduce the current. A voltmeter sits beside the component, so it must have a very high resistance, or it would take away some of the current. Mixing these up can damage the meters.

slides.heading: Quick check: connecting meters
slides.body_md: How should an ammeter and a voltmeter be connected to measure the current through a bulb and the potential difference across it?
slides.narration: Ask which meter needs the current to flow through it, and which one compares the potential at the two ends of the bulb.

slides.heading: Ohm’s law
slides.body_md: The potential difference $V$ across a metallic wire is **directly proportional to the current** $I$ through it, **provided its temperature remains the same**: $V = IR$. The constant $R$ is the **resistance**, measured in **ohm (Ω)**.

visual.alt: Table: at constant temperature, doubling the potential difference doubles the current; doubling the resistance at the same potential difference halves the current; one volt driving one ampere means a resistance of one ohm

slides.narration: Georg Simon Ohm found that for a metal wire kept at the same temperature, if you double the push, you double the current. The ratio of voltage to current stays fixed, and we call it resistance. Resistance is the opposition a conductor offers to the flow of charge. A wire has a resistance of one ohm if one volt drives one ampere through it.

slides.heading: Verifying Ohm’s law
slides.body_md: Change the current with the **rheostat**, and record the ammeter and voltmeter readings each time.

slides.narration: Here is the classic laboratory set-up. A battery drives current through a nichrome wire, an ammeter and a rheostat. The voltmeter is connected across the nichrome wire. By sliding the rheostat you change the current. For each setting, note the current and the potential difference. Keep the current small and switch off between readings, so the wire does not heat up.

slides.heading: The V–I graph
slides.body_md: Plotting $V$ against $I$ gives a **straight line through the origin**. Its **slope** $\dfrac{V}{I}$ is the **resistance**.

visual.alt: Graph of potential difference against current for a resistor: four readings at 0.3, 0.6, 0.9 and 1.2 amperes give 1.5, 3.0, 4.5 and 6.0 volts and lie on a straight line through the origin with slope 5 ohms.
visual.caption: A straight line through the origin: V is proportional to I. The slope V/I is the resistance, here 5 Ω.

slides.narration: When you plot the readings, they fall on a straight line that passes through the origin. That shape is the signature of Ohm’s law: potential difference is proportional to current. Take any point on the line and divide the voltage by the current. You get the same number every time, the resistance. A steeper line on this graph means a larger resistance.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: resistance from readings
slides.body_md: Readings for a resistor: $V$ = 1.5, 3.0, 4.5, 6.0 V and $I$ = 0.30, 0.60, 0.90, 1.20 A. Find $R$ and the current when $V = 7.5$ V.
bullets: Check — 7.5 V is $5 \times 1.5$ V, so the current should be $5 \times 0.30 = 1.5$ A. It is.

visual.alt: Table of readings: 1.5, 3.0, 4.5 and 6.0 volts with currents 0.30, 0.60, 0.90 and 1.20 amperes; the ratio V by I is 5 ohms each time

slides.narration: Always check that the ratio is constant before calling it a resistance. Here every pair gives five ohms, so the resistor obeys Ohm’s law. Predicting a new current is then easy: divide the new voltage by the resistance. A quick ratio check, like the one on the last line, catches most arithmetic slips.

slides.heading: Controlling current: the rheostat
slides.body_md: A **rheostat** is a variable resistance used to **change the current** in a circuit without changing the source. Materials with very low resistance are **good conductors**; those with very high resistance are **insulators**.
slides.narration: A rheostat is like the regulator of a ceiling fan. Turning it changes how much resistance is in the circuit, and so how much current flows. Good conductors such as copper and aluminium offer little resistance. Insulators such as rubber, plastic and glass offer so much resistance that hardly any current flows. Both have their uses: wires need conductors, and their coverings need insulators.

slides.heading: Quick check: a steeper graph
slides.body_md: Two wires give the V–I graphs shown in the question. Which has the greater resistance?
slides.narration: Look at which line rises more steeply. For the same current, which wire needs the larger potential difference?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$; 1 A = 1 C/s; conventional current flows from + to −, opposite to electrons.
Ammeter in series (low resistance); voltmeter in parallel (high resistance).
Ohm’s law: $V = IR$ at constant temperature; slope of the V–I graph is $R$.

visual.alt: Summary table of formulas and SI units: current I equals Q over t in amperes; potential difference V equals W over Q in volts; resistance R equals V over I in ohms; charge of n electrons Q equals n e in coulombs

slides.narration: Here is Part 1 on one slide. Current is charge per second. Potential difference is work per unit charge. Ammeters go in series and voltmeters in parallel. And Ohm’s law ties it together: at a constant temperature, voltage equals current times resistance. Make sure you know every unit in the table.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Convert minutes and hours to **seconds**, and mA to A, before substituting.
Write **formula → substitution → answer with unit**: typically 1 + 1 + 1 marks.
Ohm’s law statement must include "**temperature remains the same**".
Circuit diagrams: use standard symbols, show the **+ terminal** of meters towards the + of the cell, and mark the current direction.
From a V–I graph, $R = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$ — read two points far apart on the line.
slides.narration: Most lost marks in this part come from units. Students multiply amperes by minutes, or forget to convert milliamperes. Learn the exact wording of Ohm’s law, including the condition about temperature. In circuit diagrams, a missing key or a voltmeter drawn in series can cost you the whole diagram mark.

slides.heading: Resistance and resistors
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what decides the **resistance** of a wire, the idea of **resistivity**, and how resistors behave when joined **in series** and **in parallel**.
slides.narration: Why are the wires inside your house made of copper, while the coil of an electric heater is made of nichrome? Why can you switch off the fan without switching off the lights? The answers come from two ideas: what makes a wire’s resistance large or small, and what happens when several resistors are joined together. Let us work through both.

slides.heading: What decides resistance?
slides.body_md: For a wire at a given temperature, resistance is **proportional to its length** $l$ and **inversely proportional to its area of cross-section** $A$. It also depends on the **material**.

slides.narration: Imagine a crowd leaving a stadium. A longer corridor means more jostling, so a longer wire has more resistance: double the length, double the resistance. A wider corridor lets people move freely, so a thicker wire has less resistance: double the area, half the resistance. And the material matters too, which brings us to the idea of resistivity.

slides.heading: Resistivity: a property of the material
slides.body_md: Combining both, $R = \rho\,\dfrac{l}{A}$. The constant $\rho$ (rho) is the **resistivity** of the material. Its SI unit is the **ohm metre (Ω m)**. It changes with temperature but **not** with the length or thickness of the sample.

visual.alt: Table of approximate resistivities: silver 1.6, copper 1.7, aluminium 2.7 and tungsten 5.6, all times ten to the minus eight ohm metre; iron about ten to the minus seven; the alloys constantan about 4.9 times ten to the minus seven and nichrome about 1.1 times ten to the minus six; insulators such as glass and rubber from ten to the ten up to ten to the sixteen ohm metre
visual.caption: Alloys have much higher resistivity than pure metals; insulators are about 10¹⁸ or more times higher still.

slides.narration: Resistivity tells you how strongly a material itself resists current, no matter what shape you cut it into. Metals like silver and copper have tiny resistivities, which is why they make good connecting wires. Alloys such as nichrome have much higher resistivities. Insulators like glass and rubber are higher still, by a factor of about a billion billion. Cutting a wire shorter changes its resistance, but never its resistivity.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: resistance of a copper wire
slides.body_md: Find the resistance of a copper wire **20 m** long with area of cross-section **0.5 mm²**. ($\rho = 1.7 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega$ m)
bullets: Check — a long copper wire still has well under 1 Ω: that is why copper is used for wiring.

visual.alt: Table of values: resistivity 1.7 times ten to the minus eight ohm metre, length 20 metres, area 5 times ten to the minus seven square metres, resistance 0.68 ohm

slides.narration: The most common slip in these problems is the area. One square millimetre is not one thousandth of a square metre; it is one millionth, because both length and width shrink by a thousand. Convert first, then substitute. The answer, well below one ohm, makes sense for copper.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: stretching a wire
slides.body_md: A wire of resistance **3 Ω** is stretched uniformly to **twice its length**. What is its new resistance?
bullets: Step 1 — the volume of metal stays the same: $l \times A$ is constant.
Check — longer (×2) and thinner (×2): the effects multiply, giving ×4.

visual.alt: Table: before stretching, length l, area A, resistance 3 ohms; after stretching to twice the length the area halves and the resistance becomes 12 ohms

slides.narration: This is a favourite examination trap. Students double the length and say the resistance doubles. But when you stretch a wire you do not add any metal, so it must also become thinner. Twice as long and half the area: both changes increase the resistance, so it becomes four times larger.

slides.heading: Quick check: a stretched wire
slides.body_md: A wire is stretched to twice its length without changing its volume. What happens to its resistance?
slides.narration: Remember that stretching changes two things at once. Think about both before you choose.

slides.heading: Conductors, alloys and insulators at work

rows: High resistivity; does not oxidise readily when red hot

visual.alt: Table of uses: copper and aluminium for wires because of very low resistivity; nichrome for heating elements because of high resistivity and resistance to oxidation; tungsten for filaments because of its very high melting point; plastics, rubber and porcelain as insulators

slides.narration: Each job needs a material with the right resistivity. Connecting wires should waste as little energy as possible, so they use copper or aluminium. A heater element must get hot, so it uses an alloy with high resistivity that does not burn away in air at high temperature. And everything we touch is covered with an insulator, for safety.

slides.heading: Resistors in series
slides.body_md: In **series**, resistors are joined end to end. The **same current** flows through each, and the potential differences **add up**.

slides.narration: In a series circuit there is only one path, so every coulomb of charge passes through each resistor in turn. The current is the same everywhere. The battery’s potential difference is shared out: the larger the resistance, the bigger its share. On the diagram, three volts, one point eight volts and one point two volts add up to the six volts of the battery.

slides.heading: Equivalent resistance in series
slides.body_md: With the same $I$: $V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3 = IR_1 + IR_2 + IR_3$. Writing $V = IR_s$ gives the **equivalent resistance** $R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$. It is **larger than any single resistor**.

visual.alt: Table of series rules: same current through each resistor, potential differences add up, equivalent resistance is the sum, and a break anywhere stops the whole circuit

slides.narration: The derivation is short and often asked. Write the total voltage as the sum of the three voltages, replace each by current times resistance, and take the common current out. What is left is the sum of the resistances. Adding resistors in series always increases the total resistance, so the current from the same battery goes down.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a series circuit
slides.body_md: Resistors of **2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω** are joined in series to a **6 V** battery. Find the current and the potential difference across each.

visual.alt: Table of results: each resistor carries 0.6 ampere; potential differences 1.2, 1.8 and 3.0 volts, totalling 6.0 volts across 10 ohms

slides.narration: Notice the order of work: first the equivalent resistance, then the current, then each potential difference. The final check, adding the potential differences back up to the battery voltage, takes ten seconds and catches almost every mistake. In series, the biggest resistor always takes the biggest share of the voltage.

slides.heading: Quick check: what stays the same in series?
slides.body_md: Which quantity is the same for every resistor in a series combination?
slides.narration: Think about how many paths the charges have in a series circuit.

slides.heading: Resistors in parallel
slides.body_md: In **parallel**, resistors are connected between the **same two points**. Each has the **same potential difference**, and the currents **add up**.

slides.narration: Now the current has several paths, like traffic splitting at a junction into three lanes that rejoin later. Each lane, or branch, is connected across the same two points, so each gets the full potential difference. The main current divides among the branches, with the most current flowing through the branch of least resistance, and the branch currents add back up to the main current.

slides.heading: Equivalent resistance in parallel
slides.body_md: With the same $V$: $I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3 = \dfrac{V}{R_1} + \dfrac{V}{R_2} + \dfrac{V}{R_3}$. Writing $I = \dfrac{V}{R_p}$ gives $\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dfrac{1}{R_3}$. $R_p$ is **smaller than the smallest resistor**.

visual.alt: Table of parallel rules: same potential difference across each branch, currents add up, the reciprocal of the equivalent resistance is the sum of the reciprocals, and a break in one branch does not stop the others

slides.narration: Adding a branch in parallel gives the current another path, so the total resistance goes down, never up. That is why the equivalent resistance of a parallel group is always less than its smallest member. Remember to take the reciprocal at the end: a very common error is to stop at one over R and forget to flip it.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a parallel circuit
slides.body_md: Resistors of **6 Ω** and **3 Ω** are connected in parallel across a **6 V** battery. Find the equivalent resistance and the current in each branch.
bullets: Step 2 — each branch has 6 V: $I_1 = \dfrac{6}{6} = 1$ A, $I_2 = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2$ A.

visual.alt: Table: the 6 ohm branch carries 1 ampere, the 3 ohm branch carries 2 amperes, and the whole combination, 2 ohms, draws 3 amperes

slides.narration: Two routes to the total current, and they must agree: add the branch currents, or divide the voltage by the equivalent resistance. Notice that the smaller resistor carries the larger current, and that two ohms is less than either three or six ohms, exactly as the rule predicts.

slides.heading: Series and parallel together
slides.body_md: Solve **step by step**: replace each parallel group by its equivalent, then add series resistances.

Do not panic: look for the innermost group that is clearly in parallel or clearly in series, and replace it with a single equivalent resistor. Redraw the circuit in your head, and repeat until one resistor is left. Then work backwards to find each current and voltage.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a combined circuit
slides.body_md: In the circuit shown, find the total current, the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor, and the current in the 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors.
bullets: Step 1 — parallel part between P and Q: $\dfrac{6 \times 3}{6 + 3} = 2\ \Omega$.
Step 3 — across 4 Ω: $V = 2 \times 4 = 8$ V; across PQ: $V = 2 \times 2 = 4$ V.

visual.alt: Table of results: the 4 ohm resistor carries 2 amperes with 8 volts across it; the 6 ohm and 3 ohm resistors each have 4 volts and carry about 0.67 and 1.33 amperes; the whole circuit is 6 ohms drawing 2 amperes from 12 volts

slides.narration: For two resistors in parallel there is a shortcut: product divided by sum. Six times three is eighteen, six plus three is nine, so two ohms. After that it is a simple series circuit. When you work back, remember that both parallel resistors share the same four volts, so the smaller one takes more current.

slides.narration: One arrangement gives the largest total and another gives the smallest. Which is which?

slides.body_md: Each appliance gets the **full mains voltage**, draws the current it needs, and can be **switched on or off independently**.

slides.narration: Imagine your house wired in series. Switch off the fan and the lights would go off too, because the single path would be broken. And every appliance would share the two hundred and twenty volts, so none would get what it was designed for. In parallel, every branch gets the full voltage, and each has its own switch.

slides.heading: Series versus parallel for a house

rows: One appliance switched off or fails
Large: current too small for heaters
Small: each draws its own current

visual.alt: Comparison table: in series wiring the voltage is shared, one failure stops everything and the total resistance is large; in parallel wiring each appliance gets the full 220 volts, works independently and draws its own current; homes use parallel wiring

slides.narration: This comparison is a regular three-mark question. Give the reasons in pairs: what happens in series, and what happens in parallel. Remember that appliances with very different resistances, such as a bulb and a heater, need very different currents. Only parallel wiring lets each draw the current it needs.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$: $R$ increases with length, decreases with area; $\rho$ depends on the material (and temperature), unit Ω m.
Stretching a wire to $n$ times its length makes $R$ become $n^2$ times.
Series: same current, voltages add, $R_s = R_1 + R_2 + \dots$

rows: Reciprocal sum: smaller than the smallest

visual.alt: Summary table: in series the current is the same and potential differences add, giving a total larger than the largest resistor; in parallel the potential difference is the same and currents add, giving a total smaller than the smallest resistor

slides.narration: Two pictures to carry with you. A wire’s resistance depends on its length, its thickness and its material. And when resistors are combined, series adds them up while parallel brings the total down. The table tells you what stays the same and what adds up in each case.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Convert mm² to m² by multiplying by $10^{-6}$ (not $10^{-3}$).
Resistivity does **not** change when a wire is cut or stretched; resistance does.
In parallel, **take the reciprocal** at the end; check that $R_p$ is smaller than the smallest resistor.
Combined circuits: reduce step by step, then work back; check voltages add to the supply.
Derivations of $R_s$ and $R_p$ carry 2–3 marks: state what is common (current or voltage) first.
slides.narration: Three checks will protect your marks. Is my parallel answer smaller than the smallest resistor? Do my voltages add up to the battery voltage? And did I convert square millimetres properly? For derivations, examiners look for the starting statement: same current in series, same voltage in parallel. Write it clearly before the algebra.

decks.title: Electricity — Part 3: Heating effect, electric power and energy
goals: Explain the heating effect of current and apply Joule’s law H = I²Rt
Explain how fuses, heaters and filament bulbs use the heating effect
Use P = VI = I²R = V²/R to solve problems
Calculate electricity consumption in kilowatt hours and its cost

slides.heading: Heating, power and your electricity bill
slides.body_md: Part 3 — why current **heats** a wire, how we put that to use, how fast appliances use **energy** (power), and how the **units** on your bill are counted.
slides.narration: An electric iron, a kettle, a toaster and an old-style bulb all have one thing in common: they turn electrical energy into heat. Every month a meter adds up how much energy your home has used, and someone pays the bill. In this part we find out where that heat comes from, how to calculate power and energy, and how to check an electricity bill yourself.

slides.heading: Where does the heat come from?
slides.body_md: A source does work $W = VQ$ to drive charge $Q = It$ through a resistor. With $V = IR$, the energy given out as heat in time $t$ is $H = VIt = I^2Rt$. This is **Joule’s law of heating**.

visual.alt: Flow of the derivation: work done by the source equals V Q; substitute Q equals I t and V equals I R to get heat H equals I squared R t

slides.narration: When electrons push their way through a resistor, they keep colliding with its atoms and make them vibrate faster. That is heat. The energy comes from the battery or the mains, which does work on every coulomb it drives. Put together the definitions of potential difference, current and resistance, and you get Joule’s law: heat equals current squared times resistance times time.

slides.heading: Joule’s law: three factors

visual.alt: Table: heat is proportional to the square of the current, so doubling the current gives four times the heat; it is proportional to resistance and to time, so doubling either doubles the heat

slides.narration: Notice the square. Doubling the current does not double the heat, it makes it four times as large. That is why a short circuit, with its huge current, can melt wires and start fires within seconds. For the same current, the part of a circuit with the larger resistance gets hotter, which explains why a heater coil glows while its cord stays cool.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: heat in a resistor
slides.body_md: A current of **2 A** flows through a **50 Ω** resistor for **1 minute**. How much heat is produced?
bullets: Check — power is $I^2R = 200$ W; 200 J each second for 60 s is 12 000 J.

visual.alt: Table: current 2 amperes, resistance 50 ohms, time 60 seconds, heat 12 thousand joules

slides.narration: Square the current first, then multiply. Two squared is four, times fifty is two hundred, times sixty seconds is twelve thousand joules. A neat check is to find the power first, two hundred watts, which means two hundred joules every second. In one minute that adds up to the same twelve thousand joules.

slides.heading: Quick check: twice the current
slides.body_md: If the current through a heater coil is doubled, what happens to the heat produced per second?
slides.narration: Look at the power of the current in Joule’s law before you answer.

slides.heading: Putting the heating effect to work

rows: Electric iron, toaster, kettle, room heater
A coil of high resistance gets hot
Nichrome: high resistivity, does not oxidise readily
Filament gets hot enough to glow
Tungsten: melting point about 3380 °C; bulb filled with argon or nitrogen
Wire melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too large
Low melting point; connected in series

visual.alt: Table of uses: irons, toasters, kettles and heaters use a hot nichrome coil; a filament bulb uses tungsten, which melts only at about 3380 degrees Celsius, in a bulb filled with argon or nitrogen; a fuse uses a low-melting wire in series that melts when the current is too large

slides.narration: Most of the heating effect is wasted in wires and machines, but sometimes heat is exactly what we want. Heaters use coils of nichrome. A filament bulb heats tungsten until it glows white; most of the energy still comes out as heat, which is why LED bulbs save so much electricity. And a fuse uses heat to protect us, by melting when the current becomes dangerous.

slides.body_md: The **filament** is a fine coil of **tungsten** in a bulb of **inert gas**. A **fuse** is a short wire of **low melting point** placed **in series**.

Right: a cartridge fuse, a thin fuse wire of low melting point running between two metal caps inside a glass or porcelain tube; it is connected in series with the circuit it protects.

slides.narration: Look at the coiled filament: coiling packs a long, thin, high-resistance wire into a small space. The bulb is filled with argon or nitrogen, which do not react with hot tungsten, so the filament lasts longer. On the right is a cartridge fuse. All the current passes through its thin wire. If the current rises too high, the wire heats up, melts, and the circuit is broken.

slides.heading: Fuse ratings
slides.body_md: A fuse is chosen with a rating **a little above the normal current** of the circuit. Common ratings are **1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and 15 A**. The normal current is found from $I = \dfrac{P}{V}$.
slides.narration: A fuse must survive the normal current but melt quickly if the current becomes much larger, as in a short circuit or an overload. So we calculate the normal current of the appliance and choose the next standard rating above it. A fuse that is too small keeps blowing; a fuse that is too large gives no protection at all. Never replace a fuse with ordinary copper wire.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: choosing a fuse
slides.body_md: A room heater is rated **2 kW, 220 V**. Which fuse should its circuit have: 5 A, 10 A or 15 A?
bullets: Step 3 — 5 A would blow at once; 15 A is far above the normal current.

visual.alt: Table comparing fuses with the heater’s normal current of 9.1 amperes: 5 ampere blows in normal use, 10 ampere is just above and correct, 15 ampere gives poor protection

slides.narration: The heater draws a little over nine amperes. A five ampere fuse would melt as soon as you switched on. A fifteen ampere fuse would let a dangerous current flow before it melted. Ten amperes is the right choice: just above the normal current. This is exactly the reasoning an electrician uses.

slides.heading: Quick check: how a fuse is connected
slides.body_md: What kind of wire is used in a fuse, and how is the fuse connected?
slides.narration: For a fuse to protect a circuit, all the current must pass through it. And it must melt before anything else is damaged.

slides.heading: Electric power
slides.body_md: **Power** is the rate at which electrical energy is used: $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = VI$. Using $V = IR$, $P = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$. Unit: **watt (W)**; 1 W = 1 J/s = 1 V × 1 A; **1 kW = 1000 W**.

visual.alt: Table: use P equals V I when voltage and current are known, P equals I squared R when current and resistance are known, as in series circuits, and P equals V squared over R when voltage and resistance are known, as in parallel circuits

slides.narration: Power tells you how fast an appliance uses energy. A one thousand watt iron uses a thousand joules every second. You have three forms of the formula, all equally correct. Pick the one that matches what you know. In a series circuit the current is common, so I squared R is handy. Across the mains, the voltage is common, so V squared over R is handy.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a bulb’s current and resistance
slides.body_md: A bulb is rated **40 W, 220 V**. Find the current it draws and its resistance when glowing.

visual.alt: Table: a 40 watt, 220 volt bulb draws about 0.18 ampere and has a resistance of 1210 ohms when glowing

slides.narration: A rating such as forty watts, two hundred and twenty volts means the bulb uses forty watts only when connected to two hundred and twenty volts. From these two numbers you can find both its current and its resistance. Notice that a lower-wattage bulb has a higher resistance: power and resistance go opposite ways when the voltage is fixed.

slides.heading: Electrical energy and the kilowatt hour
slides.body_md: Energy used $E = Pt$. The commercial unit is the **kilowatt hour (kWh)**, the energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour. On bills it is called **one unit**. $1\ \text{kWh} = 1000\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J.

visual.alt: Table: one unit, one kilowatt hour, is used by a 1000 watt iron in 1 hour, a 100 watt television in 10 hours and a 10 watt LED bulb in 100 hours

slides.narration: The joule is far too small for household use: a single iron uses millions of joules in an hour. So electricity boards use a bigger unit, the kilowatt hour, which they simply call a unit. One unit is enough to run a one kilowatt iron for an hour, or a ten watt LED bulb for a hundred hours. Note carefully: the kilowatt hour is a unit of energy, not of power.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a month’s electricity bill
slides.body_md: The Sharma family’s daily use is shown. At **₹6 per unit**, what is their bill for **30 days**?
bullets: Step 1 — energy per day = $5 \times 10 \times 6 + 2 \times 60 \times 10 + 100 \times 3 + 2000 \times 0.5 = 2800$ Wh $= 2.8$ kWh.
Step 2 — energy in 30 days = $2.8 \times 30 = 84$ kWh, that is, 84 units.
Check — the fans and the geyser use 2.2 of the 2.8 units each day: those are the places to save.

visual.alt: Table of a household’s daily use: five 10 watt LED bulbs for 6 hours use 300 watt hours; two 60 watt fans for 10 hours use 1200 watt hours; a 100 watt television for 3 hours uses 300 watt hours; a 2000 watt geyser for half an hour uses 1000 watt hours; the total is 2800 watt hours, or 2.8 kilowatt hours, per day

slides.narration: Work appliance by appliance: power times number times hours gives watt hours. Add them up and divide by a thousand to get units. Multiply by thirty days, then by the rate. Look at which appliances dominate. Here the fans, running ten hours a day, use more than the geyser, even though the geyser’s power is much larger. Time matters as much as power.

slides.heading: Quick check: the kilowatt hour
slides.body_md: How many joules are there in one kilowatt hour?
slides.narration: Write one kilowatt as watts and one hour as seconds, then multiply.

slides.heading: Which bulb glows brighter?
slides.body_md: For a fixed voltage, $R = \dfrac{V^2}{P}$: the **lower-wattage bulb has the higher resistance**. Brightness depends on the power **actually used** in the circuit.

visual.alt: Table: a 100 watt bulb has 484 ohms and a 60 watt bulb about 807 ohms; in parallel on 220 volts each uses its full rating and the 100 watt bulb is brighter; in series the same current flows, so the 60 watt bulb, with larger resistance, uses more power and is brighter

slides.narration: Here is a puzzle examiners love. Connect a hundred watt and a sixty watt bulb in parallel across the mains, and the hundred watt bulb is brighter, as you would expect. Now connect them in series. The same current flows through both, so the bulb with the larger resistance uses more power. That is the sixty watt bulb, which now glows brighter.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Heating devices use nichrome; filaments use tungsten in inert gas; fuses melt and break the circuit.
Power $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$, in watts.

visual.alt: Summary table: heat H equals I squared R t in joules; power P equals V I, I squared R or V squared over R in watts; energy E equals P t in joules or kilowatt hours

slides.narration: Part 3 in a nutshell. Current heats a resistor according to Joule’s law. We use that heat in heaters, bulbs and fuses. Power is the rate of using energy, with three equivalent formulas. Energy is power times time, and on your bill it is counted in kilowatt hours, called units.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In $H = I^2Rt$ and $E = Pt$, use **seconds** for joules but **hours** for kWh; never mix them.
kWh is a unit of **energy**, not power; 1 kWh = $3.6 \times 10^6$ J.
Fuse: **low melting point**, **in series**, rating just above the normal current.
Bill questions: show energy per appliance, total units, then cost — 1 mark each.
For brightness puzzles, find $R = V^2/P$ for each bulb, then use $I^2R$ (series) or $V^2/R$ (parallel).
slides.narration: The deadliest slip in this part is mixing units: watts with hours gives watt hours, not joules. Decide at the start whether you want joules or kilowatt hours, and convert accordingly. For bill questions, set out the working in a table, as we did; examiners award marks step by step. And for any fuse question, mention both the low melting point and the series connection.

notes.title: Electricity — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Electric current, potential difference and circuit diagrams
sections.body_md:
**Electric current** is the rate of flow of charge: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$. SI unit **ampere** (1 A = 1 C/s); 1 mA $= 10^{-3}$ A, 1 μA $= 10^{-6}$ A. In metal wires the moving charges are **electrons**; **conventional current** is taken from the + terminal to the − terminal, opposite to electron flow. Charge of an electron $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C; $Q = n e$, and 1 C is the charge of about $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.

**Potential difference** between two points is the work done to move a unit charge between them: $V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$. SI unit **volt** (1 V = 1 J/C). A cell maintains a potential difference by chemical action.

**Measuring:** an **ammeter** (very low resistance) is connected **in series**; a **voltmeter** (very high resistance) **in parallel** across the component. The + terminal of each meter is connected towards the + terminal of the cell.

**Circuit symbols:** cell (long thin line +, short thick line −), battery, plug key (open/closed), wire joint, wires crossing without joining, bulb, resistor (zigzag), rheostat (zigzag with arrow), ammeter, voltmeter.

The potential difference when 1 J of work moves 1 C of charge.

sections.heading: 2. Ohm’s law and resistance
sections.body_md:
**Ohm’s law:** the potential difference across a metallic wire is directly proportional to the current through it, provided its **temperature remains the same**: $V = IR$.

**Resistance** $R = \dfrac{V}{I}$ is the opposition a conductor offers to the flow of charge. SI unit **ohm** (1 Ω = 1 V/1 A). The V–I graph of an ohmic conductor is a **straight line through the origin**; its **slope** (V on the y-axis) is $R$, so a steeper line means a larger resistance.

**Verification:** battery, plug key, ammeter, nichrome wire and rheostat in series, voltmeter across the wire; vary the current with the rheostat, record V and I, plot V against I. Keep currents small so the wire does not heat up.

A **rheostat** (variable resistance) changes the current without changing the source. **Good conductors** have low resistance; **insulators** very high.

key_terms.definition_md: V is proportional to I for a conductor at constant temperature.
The ratio V/I; the property of a conductor that opposes current; SI unit ohm.
A variable resistance used to change the current in a circuit.

sections.heading: 3. Factors affecting resistance; resistivity
sections.body_md:
At a given temperature, $R \propto l$ and $R \propto \dfrac{1}{A}$, so $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$. **Resistivity** $\rho$ depends on the **material** and **temperature**, not on the length or thickness; SI unit **Ω m**.

- Cutting a wire into $n$ equal pieces gives $\dfrac{R}{n}$ each.
- Stretching a wire to $n$ times its length (volume constant) makes its area $\dfrac{A}{n}$, so $R$ becomes $n^2 R$.
- Metals and alloys: about $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-6}$ Ω m; insulators: about $10^{12}$ to $10^{17}$ Ω m.
- **Alloys** have higher resistivity than their constituent metals and do not oxidise readily at high temperature, so they are used in heating devices (nichrome). **Copper and aluminium** (low resistivity) are used for wires; **tungsten** (very high melting point) for filaments.

Remember to convert mm² to m² by multiplying by $10^{-6}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit area of cross-section; a property of the material; SI unit ohm metre.
A mixture of metals such as nichrome or constantan; higher resistivity than its constituent metals.

sections.heading: 4. Resistors in series and in parallel
sections.body_md:
**Series:** the **same current** flows through each resistor; potential differences add: $V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$. Equivalent resistance $R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$, larger than the largest. A break anywhere stops the whole circuit.

**Parallel:** the **same potential difference** acts across each resistor; currents add: $I = I_1 + I_2 + I_3$. $\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dfrac{1}{R_3}$, smaller than the smallest. For two resistors, $R_p = \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$.

**Combined circuits:** replace each parallel or series group by its equivalent, find the total current, then work back to each current and potential difference. Check that voltages add up to the supply and currents add up at junctions.

**Household wiring is parallel**: each appliance gets the full 220 V, draws the current it needs and can be switched independently; in series, one fault would stop everything and the voltage would be shared.

sections.heading: 5. Heating effect of electric current
sections.body_md:
The energy supplied by the source in driving current through a resistor is dissipated as **heat**: $H = VIt = I^2Rt$ (**Joule’s law of heating**). Heat is proportional to the **square of the current**, to the **resistance** and to the **time**.

**Applications:** electric iron, toaster, kettle and room heater (nichrome coils); **incandescent bulb** — a tungsten filament (melting point about 3380 °C) glows white-hot in a bulb filled with **argon or nitrogen** to prolong its life; most of the energy still becomes heat. **Electric fuse** — a wire of **low melting point** connected **in series**; it melts when the current exceeds the safe value, breaking the circuit. Common ratings: 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 and 15 A; choose the rating just above the normal current $I = P/V$.

**Unwanted heating** wastes energy in wires, motors and electronic devices and can cause fires in overloaded circuits.

key_terms.definition_md: Heat produced in a resistor equals I squared R t.
A safety device: a wire of low melting point in series that melts when the current is too large.

sections.heading: 6. Electric power and energy
sections.body_md:
**Electric power** is the rate at which electrical energy is used: $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$. SI unit **watt** (1 W = 1 J/s = 1 V × 1 A); 1 kW = 1000 W.

**Energy** $E = Pt$. Commercial unit: **kilowatt hour** (one "unit") $= 1000\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J. The kWh is a unit of **energy**, not power.

**Bills:** energy per appliance = power × number × hours; add, convert Wh to kWh, multiply by days and by the rate per unit.

**Ratings:** "P watts, V volts" means P is used only at V. For a fixed voltage, $R = V^2/P$: a lower-wattage bulb has a higher resistance. In **parallel**, each gets the full voltage and the higher-wattage bulb is brighter; in **series**, the same current flows and the bulb with the **higher resistance** (lower wattage) is brighter.

key_terms.definition_md: Rate of using electrical energy; SI unit watt.
Energy used by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour; 3.6 million joules; one unit on bills.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using minutes or hours in $Q = It$ or $H = I^2Rt$ (use **seconds** for coulombs and joules); using seconds when the answer is wanted in **kWh** (use hours and kW).
- Converting mm² to m² with $10^{-3}$ instead of $10^{-6}$.
- Leaving out "at constant temperature" from Ohm’s law.
- Saying resistivity changes when a wire is cut or stretched (only resistance changes); forgetting the area also changes when a wire is stretched.
- Forgetting to take the reciprocal for parallel resistances; check $R_p$ is less than the smallest.
- Drawing a voltmeter in series or an ammeter in parallel; missing the plug key or + terminals.
- Calling the kWh a unit of power.
- Fuse answers without both "**low melting point**" and "**in series**".

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Numericals: formula (1) + correct substitution with units converted (1) + answer with unit (1).
- Derivations (series/parallel, Joule’s law, $P = VI$): starting statement (1) + steps (1–2).
- Circuit diagrams: correct symbols and connections (1), meters correctly placed with polarity (1).
- Bill questions: energy per appliance (1) + total units (1) + cost (1).
- Case-based questions: two 1-mark parts from the passage and a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

cards.front_md: Define electric current and give its SI unit.
cards.back_md: Rate of flow of charge, $I = Q/t$; **ampere** (1 A = 1 C/s).

cards.front_md: Direction of conventional current vs electron flow
cards.back_md: Conventional current: **+ to −** through the circuit; electrons move **− to +**.

cards.front_md: Charge of one electron
cards.back_md: $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C; 1 C ≈ $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.

cards.front_md: Define potential difference and 1 volt.
cards.back_md: Work done per unit charge, $V = W/Q$; 1 V = **1 J/C**.

cards.front_md: How are an ammeter and a voltmeter connected?
cards.back_md: Ammeter **in series** (low resistance); voltmeter **in parallel** (high resistance).

cards.front_md: Symbol for a cell: which plate is positive?
cards.back_md: The **longer, thinner** line is +; the shorter, thicker line is −.

cards.front_md: State Ohm’s law.
cards.back_md: V across a metallic wire is proportional to I through it, **provided the temperature remains the same**: $V = IR$.

cards.front_md: What does the slope of a V–I graph give?
cards.back_md: The **resistance** (V on the y-axis); steeper line = larger R.

cards.front_md: 1 ohm
cards.back_md: Resistance of a conductor through which 1 A flows when 1 V is applied.

cards.front_md: What is a rheostat used for?
cards.back_md: To **change the current** in a circuit without changing the source.

cards.front_md: Formula linking R, ρ, l and A
cards.back_md: $R = \rho \dfrac{l}{A}$

cards.front_md: SI unit of resistivity; does it depend on the length of the wire?
cards.back_md: **Ω m**; no — it depends only on the material and temperature.

cards.front_md: A wire is stretched to twice its length. New resistance?
cards.back_md: **4R** (length ×2, area ÷2).

cards.front_md: Why is nichrome used in heating elements?
cards.back_md: High resistivity and does not oxidise readily at high temperature.

cards.front_md: Why are copper and aluminium used for wires?
cards.back_md: Very **low resistivity**: little energy is wasted.

cards.front_md: Series: what is common, what adds, and R_s?
cards.back_md: Same **current**; voltages add; $R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$.

cards.front_md: Parallel: what is common, what adds, and R_p?
cards.back_md: Same **voltage**; currents add; $\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}$.

cards.front_md: Two resistors in parallel: shortcut
Three 6 Ω resistors: largest and smallest combinations?
cards.back_md: 18 Ω (series) and 2 Ω (parallel).

cards.front_md: Why are homes wired in parallel?
cards.back_md: Each appliance gets the **full 220 V**, draws its own current and can be **switched independently**.

cards.front_md: State Joule’s law of heating.
cards.back_md: $H = I^2Rt$: heat ∝ square of current, resistance and time.

cards.front_md: Doubling the current makes the heat…
cards.back_md: **Four times** as large.

cards.front_md: Two properties of a fuse wire and its connection
cards.back_md: **Low melting point**; connected **in series**.

cards.front_md: Why is a bulb filled with argon or nitrogen?
cards.back_md: To stop the hot tungsten filament from **oxidising**, prolonging its life.

cards.front_md: Why does a heater element glow but its cord does not?
cards.back_md: Same current, but the element has a **much higher resistance**, so far more heat ($I^2R$).

cards.front_md: Three formulas for electric power
cards.back_md: $P = VI = I^2R = \dfrac{V^2}{R}$

cards.front_md: 1 kWh in joules
Is kWh a unit of power?
cards.back_md: No — it is a unit of **energy**.

cards.front_md: Resistance of a 100 W, 220 V bulb
100 W and 60 W bulbs in series on 220 V: which is brighter?
cards.back_md: The **60 W** bulb: same current, larger resistance, so larger $I^2R$.

questions.stem_md: A current of 1 ampere in a wire means that

options.text_md: 1 coulomb of charge passes any cross-section of the wire every second
1 electron passes any cross-section of the wire every second
1 joule of energy is given to each coulomb of charge
1 volt is applied across the wire

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$, so 1 A = 1 C/s.
Step 2: So 1 coulomb passes each cross-section every second (a).
Step 3: One electron per second (b) is a tiny current of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ A. 1 J per coulomb (c) defines the volt, and (d) is a potential difference, not a current.

questions.stem_md: In a torch, a cell lights a bulb. Which statement about the direction of flow is correct?

options.text_md: Electrons and conventional current both flow from the + terminal to the − terminal
Conventional current flows from + to − through the bulb, while electrons flow from − to +
Electrons flow from + to −, and conventional current from − to +
There is no direction: charges vibrate back and forth

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: By convention, current flows from the positive terminal through the external circuit to the negative terminal.
Step 2: In metals the moving charges are electrons, which carry negative charge and move the opposite way, from − to +. So (b).
Step 3: (a) and (c) put the two flows in the same or reversed wrong directions; (d) describes alternating current, not a torch cell.

questions.stem_md: A mobile phone charger delivers a steady current of 2 A for 30 minutes. How much charge flows into the phone?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: $t = 30 \times 60 = 1800$ s.
Step 2: $Q = It = 2 \times 1800 = 3600$ C, so (c).
Step 3: (a) uses minutes instead of seconds; (b) divides instead of multiplying by 2; (d) doubles the time.

questions.stem_md: To measure the current through a bulb and the potential difference across it, Ravi should connect

options.text_md: both the ammeter and the voltmeter in series with the bulb
the ammeter in parallel and the voltmeter in series with the bulb
both meters in parallel with the bulb
the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel with the bulb

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The current to be measured must pass through the ammeter, so it goes in series.
Step 2: The voltmeter compares the potential at the two ends of the bulb, so it goes in parallel across it. So (d).
Step 3: A voltmeter in series (a, b) would allow almost no current; an ammeter in parallel (b, c) would short-circuit the bulb.

questions.stem_md: A current of 0.4 A flows through a bulb for 5 minutes. How much charge passes through it, in coulombs?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: $t = 5 \times 60 = 300$ s.
Step 2: $Q = It = 0.4 \times 300 = 120$ C.
Answer: 120 C.

questions.stem_md: A wire carries a current of 0.8 A. How many electrons pass a point in the wire each second? Give your answer as a multiple of $10^{18}$. ($e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Charge passing each second: $Q = It = 0.8 \times 1 = 0.8$ C.
Step 2: $n = \dfrac{Q}{e} = \dfrac{0.8}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.5 \times 10^{19} = 5 \times 10^{18}$.
Answer: 5 (that is, $5 \times 10^{18}$ electrons each second).

questions.stem_md: How much work, in joules, is done in moving 15 C of charge across two points that have a potential difference of 9 V?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: $V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$, so $W = VQ$.
Step 2: $W = 9 \times 15 = 135$ J.
Answer: 135 J.

questions.stem_md: One volt is the potential difference when one joule of work is done to move one ___ of charge between two points.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: $V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$.
Step 2: 1 V = 1 J per coulomb, so the answer is coulomb.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A good ammeter has a very high resistance.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: An ammeter is connected in series, so all the current passes through it.
Step 2: To avoid reducing the current it measures, it must have a very low resistance. The statement is false (a voltmeter has a very high resistance).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An ammeter is always connected in series with the component whose current is to be measured.

**Reason (R):** A voltmeter has a very high resistance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The current must pass through the ammeter, so it is connected in series: A is true.
Step 2: A voltmeter does have a very high resistance: R is true.
Step 3: R is about the voltmeter; it does not explain how an ammeter is connected. So (b).

questions.stem_md: Match each physical quantity with its SI unit.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Current — ampere (p–3).
Step 2: Potential difference — volt (q–4).
Step 3: Charge — coulomb (r–1).
Step 4: Resistance — ohm (s–2).

questions.stem_md: Define potential difference between two points in a circuit. What is meant by saying that the potential difference between two points is 1 volt?

answer.model_answer_md: The **potential difference** between two points is the **work done to move a unit charge** from one point to the other: $V = \dfrac{W}{Q}$. A potential difference of **1 volt** means that **1 joule of work** is done in moving **1 coulomb** of charge between the two points.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Define V as work done per unit charge.
Step 2: Interpret 1 V = 1 J/C.

1 V: 1 J of work per 1 C of charge

questions.stem_md: A torch cell has a potential difference of 1.5 V across its terminals. How much energy does it give to each coulomb of charge that passes through the bulb?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: $W = VQ = 1.5 \times 1 = 1.5$ J, so (a).
Step 2: (b) inverts the relation ($Q/V$), (c) doubles it, and (d) is ten times too large.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define electric current and state its SI unit.
(b) A current of 0.6 A flows through a bulb for 5 minutes. Find the charge that flows and the number of electrons that pass. ($e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C)
(c) Describe, in words, a circuit to measure the current through a resistor and the potential difference across it. Name the components.
(d) Why should a voltmeter have a very high resistance?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Electric current** is the rate of flow of charge, $I = \dfrac{Q}{t}$. SI unit: **ampere** (1 A = 1 C/s).

(b) $t = 5 \times 60 = 300$ s; $Q = It = 0.6 \times 300 = 180$ C. $n = \dfrac{Q}{e} = \dfrac{180}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.125 \times 10^{21}$ electrons.

(c) A **cell (or battery)**, a **plug key**, an **ammeter** and the **resistor** are joined **in series**; a **voltmeter** is connected **in parallel across the resistor**. The + terminals of both meters are joined towards the + terminal of the cell. Closing the key, the ammeter reads the current and the voltmeter the potential difference.

(d) The voltmeter is connected across the component; with a very high resistance it **draws almost no current**, so it does not change the current or potential difference it is measuring.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Define current and its unit.
Step 2: Convert time, use $Q = It$, then $n = Q/e$.
Step 3: Describe the series loop with the voltmeter in parallel.
Step 4: Explain why a high resistance avoids disturbing the circuit.

questions.stem_md: Ohm’s law, $V \propto I$, holds for a metallic wire only if

options.text_md: its temperature and other physical conditions remain the same
the wire is made of copper
the potential difference is less than 1 V

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ohm’s law states that V is proportional to I provided the temperature (and other physical conditions) of the conductor stay the same.
Step 2: So (b).
Step 3: Large currents (a) heat the wire and can make the law fail; the law is not limited to copper (c) or to small voltages (d).

assets.alt: V–I graphs of two wires: wire A is a straight line from the origin reaching 10 volts at 1 ampere; wire B is a less steep straight line reaching 4 volts at 1 ampere.
